title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor takes legal action over search warrants before his arrest
description: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over his arrest in February.The former Prince Andrew was arrested on su
body: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking legal action against Thames Valley Police over his arrest in February.The former Prince Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the United States.Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are challenging the search warrants used in Sandringham and at Royal Lodge in Windsor relating to his arrest, as first reported by the Telegraph.Thames Valley Police confirmed: "We are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court.""As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further," a spokesperson for the force that carried out the arrest said.Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants.A court hearing will be held on Thursday afternoon to begin considering this bid to quash the warrants, with the hearing set to begin in private. The judge will initially hear a request by the police to keep some documents private.The warrants had been issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February - the day before Mountbatten-Windsor had been arrested - and the legal challenge is against the chief constable of Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court."Even if Andrew succeeds in having the search warrants quashed, that would not necessarily be the victory it might first appear," said Nick Vamos, a criminal lawyer at Peters & Peters and former head of special crime at the Crown Prosecution Service.Vamos said such disputes over warrants were not uncommon - but if the police lost on a technical error, they could still sometimes keep what they had obtained in a search."The police can apply back to the Crown Court to retain the material if they have grounds to immediately seize it again," said Vamos.It would need to be a more fundamental issue with the granting of the warrants for the police to be required to return the material from a search, he said.For several days after the arrest, police were seen searching Mountbatten-Windsor's property at Marsh Farm in Sandringham and at his former home, Royal Lodge, on the Windsor estate.The arrest, carried out on his 66th birthday, followed a series of revelations from the Epstein files, published by the US Department of Justice.They included emails appearing to show official documents being shared by Mountbatten-Windsor with Epstein and others, at a time when he was the UK's trade envoy.Mountbatten-Windsor had already been stripped of his titles by King Charles, after emails had shown Mountbatten-Windsor had continued his links with Epstein, beyond when he had publicly said those links had been severed.After Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February he was taken to Aylsham police station. A photograph captured his departure later that day, looking exhausted, after he was released under investigation. The launch of this legal action against the police over the search warrants is the first public pushback from the former prince, who has lost his home, titles and public status, with charities and businesses distancing themselves from him.Thames Valley Police says its investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is continuing. In a previous update it said the force had been "working with the United States Department of Justice to get further information that may be related to this investigation".Detectives also highlighted that allegations of sexual misconduct could be considered as part of this inquiry into potential misconduct in public office.Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing in his associations with Epstein.

schema.headline: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor takes legal action over search warrants before his arrest

title: All passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast
description: Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, accordi
body: Six people aboard a medical transport aircraft that went missing on Saturday while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston are presumed dead, according to a statement from the flight's operator.On Sunday evening, the United States Coast Guard said it was ending its search for survivors off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island."We must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died," Latitude Air Ambulance said in a statement shortly thereafter."Our thoughts are first and foremost with their families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues."The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday morning.On Saturday evening, authorities located a "debris field" confirmed to be from the aircraft.The plane had departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time on Friday night, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).Four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals were onboard."This is an unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people aboard Heartbeat 104," said Peter Byl, President of Latitude Air Ambulance, on Sunday evening. "Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."Latitude Air Ambulance is a Canadian company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.Two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, had flown to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News. FlightAware's tracker shows that the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).Radio transmissions show trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported, based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net. "You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?" the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"The pilot's response was inaudible."You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe. The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue". The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".Latitude said in its statement on Sunday evening that it would continue to cooperate with relevant authorities during ongoing recovery efforts and investigations. "Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

schema.headline: All passengers presumed dead after plane went missing off US coast

title: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' conference motion
description: Israel's foreign ministry says it has banned Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, after party members adopted a motion declarin
body: Israel's foreign ministry says it has banned Green Party leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, after party members adopted a motion declaring Zionism a form of racism.Israel's foreign ministry described the motion as a "clear antisemitic text" and beyond "the boundaries of legitimate political debate".Polanski did not take part in the vote on Sunday. The motion, which has divided senior party figures, defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".It has been criticised by some Jewish groups, who called the motion an "attack on the Jewish community"."Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it," the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council  said in a statement."Branding most British Jews and Jewish institutions 'racist' stokes anti-Jewish hatred after a year in which British Jews have been murdered attending their synagogue, stabbed in the streets, and seen their community buildings firebombed."Israel's foreign ministry said the motion was "a stain on the history of the United Kingdom".The party's joint deputy leaders have been at odds over the subject, with Mothin Ali backing the move, and Rachel Millward describing the wording as "problematic".But members endorsed the policy motion, which was put forward by a group of activists at the party's conference in Brighton, by 1,022 votes to 813."The real, material, manifestation of Zionism has been the historic and ongoing dehumanisation, displacement, dispossession, disenfranchisement and destruction of Palestinians," it says.Discussion about the vote has dominated the conference, and exposed divisions between the party's newly enlarged membership base under Polanski and its MPs elected at the last general  election. Speaking after the vote, Lubna Speitan, the Green member behind the motion, argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression"."We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions," she added. Polanski did not vote in the debate, having left the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras, where he is standing in a by-election to be the MP. A full list of candidates in the contest can be found here. Asked about the motion on Friday, Polanski said: "If your Zionism is the displacement of the Palestinian people then that is clearly racist, and I say that as a Jewish leader of a British political party."However, he said he wanted to see the reference to a single Palestinian state changed, arguing: "I don't believe we as a Green Party of England and Wales, or even the British government, should be deciding what the future settlement looks like."He had also said he wanted to see the motion amended to specify that it should not be used to discipline Jewish members attending synagogues that consider themselves Zionist.However, both amendments favoured by Polanski were rejected by Green members.The Board of Deputies and the Jewish Leadership Council statement referred to a "particular criticism" for Polanski "who neither spoke against the motion nor voted" but welcomed the subsequent "cross-party condemnation".A Green spokeswoman insisted the party would protect Jewish members - and they would not be persecuted for attending synagogues which defined themselves as Zionist.Speaking after the motion had been approved, Vivien Lichtenstein, chairwoman of Jewish Greens,  told the BBC she could consider her future in the party. Polanski has not specified whether he supports the motion passed by members, but added his name to a joint statement from the party's five MPs and deputy leaders issued after the vote.The statement pledged to ensure the Green Party was "an anti-racist party in every way" and added that there was "no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people".Over the course of the three-day conference, key figures in the party have expressed differing positions about the Zionism motion. Four of the party's five MPs - Ellie Chowns, Adrian Ramsay and Carla Denyer, Sian Berry - had publicly opposed it, with Denyer arguing it could risk "alienating a significant proportion of Jewish people".Chowns, as well as former Green Party leader Caroline Lucas, both spoke against the motion during the debate.Addressing members, Lucas said: "I urge you not to support the over-simplification at the heart of this motion - a refusal to accept complexities which is leading to so many Jewish members feeling scared and unwelcome in our party."Deputy leader Mothin Ali, who had expressed support for the motion before the vote, said it was calling for "a state that's democratic, that guarantees the rights of every single person living on that land".He added that he was "absolutely not" calling all Jewish people who define themselves as Zionists racist.Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election. Labour chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said the vote "crosses a line" and called on Polanski to "make clear that this will not be their position moving forwards"."It is shameful to vote against a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine and to condemn the vast majority of British Jews and Jews around the world as racist for supporting Israel's right to exist," she added.Shadow home secretary Chris Philp criticised the motion on behalf of the Conservatives, saying it demonstrated the Green Party was "toxic to its core". "British Jews should not have to disclaim a belief in Jewish self-determination and the existence of Israel in order to be accepted by a British political party", he said.Liberal Democrat MP Luke Taylor said the motion did not address "the rising threats" of Islamophobia and antisemitism in the UK.He added: "This is a divisive motion that pours fuel on the fire of tensions in the UK, and will leave many British Jews feeling less safe."

schema.headline: Green Party members back 'Zionism is racism' conference motion

title: Up to 500 schools close in France over student protests
description: Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days,
body: Up to 500 schools across France will be partially or totally closed on Monday after clashes between riot police and student protesters in recent days, the French education minister said on Sunday.Lessons will be "totally or partly suspended" in some "400 to 500" high schools as security conditions "have not been fulfilled", Édouard Geffray said. He also said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" since the start of the protests. Thousands of students have been demonstrating over education standards and the protests, which started last week, have spread from Paris to other cities, including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille.High school pupils and others have objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.On Friday, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 735 of France's 3,700 schools had been affected "one way or another" by violent protests.The education minister warned the number of schools potentially affected on Monday could be comparable to Friday's figure but promised a "partial, progressive return to lessons"."There are activists - particularly from the far-left - who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Édouard Geffray claimed."Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he said. Geffray added that 78 staff members in education had been wounded, which he described as "something we have never seen before".On Friday 1,747 people were arrested, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. Over 5,000 people have been arrested altogether since the start of the movement, according the AFP news agency, with around 85% of them minors.

schema.headline: Up to 500 schools close in France over student protests

title: The job interview question you don't have to answer
description: Figure caption, Watch: How much is your salary?ByCost of living correspondentPrepare all you like, but there is often still one job interview question
body: Figure caption, Watch: How much is your salary?ByCost of living correspondentPrepare all you like, but there is often still one job interview question that leaves you feeling uncomfortable.While employers in the UK are within their rights to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, applicants are not obliged to tell them.Recruiters have been encouraged to stop posing questions about salary history and, in the EU, new rules will prevent them doing so.But in the UK, there is still a chance of it coming up, so how best should you answer?What can interviewers ask?Sometimes it feels like interviewers, and interviewees, tip-toe around the subject of money.But Louise Rudd, a senior adviser at the workplace advice and conciliation service Acas, says there are no regulations that prevent employers from asking interviewees about their current salary, or their salary expectations.She says employers, if they do want to know, should ask each applicant the same questions to ensure they are treated fairly.A few years ago, a campaign was launched urging employers to stop asking new recruits how much they were paid in their previous jobs. It had its own hashtag - #EndSalaryHistory.The Fawcett Society, which campaigns for women and gender equality, said that asking the question risked maintaining historic unfair differences in pay due to gender, race and disability inequality. Rather than offering a salary based on skills, experience and performance, it meant employers rewarded an individual's perceived worth and negotiating skills instead, the society said.Image source, Getty ImagesThe Recruitment and Employment Confederation supported the move, urging recruiters not to ask.Employers in the EU will be banned from asking about salary history in new rules being rolled out across the bloc.But that's not featured in Cabinet Office plans in the UK, which instead concentrates on telling employers to publish salary information in job adverts.What's the best way to answer?When you're going for a new job, you can reveal your current salary if you are happy to.Some people asked by BBC News out and about in London suggested they would reply with an inflated salary - so they get paid more in the next job. However, the risks of lying in an interview can far outweigh the possible reward.There are no requirements for you to disclose your salary if you don't want to.Rudd says some people might prefer to give their salary expectations, or outline their understanding of the salary range for the role.Recruitment firms often say applicants could instead focus on their skills and experience, so those are used as a measure of what they should be paid, not their salary history. Shazia Ejaz, director of campaigns at the Recruitment and Employment Confederation, says jobseekers should approach questions about pay with "realism but also confidence". "Candidates can focus on showcasing the value they bring, the benefits that matter most to them and to go to the interview knowing the market rate for the role," she says."Jobseekers who have done their homework on salaries and can explain the contribution they will make are in the strongest position to secure the right package."Get in touchWhat was your worst job interview? How did you handle it?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: The job interview question you don't have to answer

title: Trump chooses top spy boss to run new AI taskforce
description: US President Donald Trump has named the director of national intelligence as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will coordinate governm
body: US President Donald Trump has named the director of national intelligence as the head of a new taskforce on AI which, he said, will coordinate government engagement with consumers, companies and "religious organizations".Jay Clayton will head a taskforce that has drawn criticism from the likes of Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren who has called for regulation of AI.Trump has rejected the idea of laws to control development of the technology despite a debate about the potential risks of AI and what it means for humanity.Last week, the president and the heads of major AI firms signed a "morally binding" document, making them responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology.Trump - who is unilaterally attempting to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" - wrote on social media: "The Super Intelligence Force will coordinate the Federal Government's engagement with Consumers, Public Interest Groups, Religious Organizations, Critical Infrastructure Providers, and Super Intelligence Companies." As well as Clayton, a former chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission,  Andrew Ferguson, head of the Federal Trade Commission, will be on the taskforce along with Emil Michael, undersecretary of defense for research and engineering.It will report directly to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.Trump has pushed back against any kind of slowdown on AI development. He said the US is leading the race ahead of China, adding: "And, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."President Xi Jinping recently travelled to Washington for a state visit. Days later, Trump ruled out a joint venture between the US and China to develop AI."If we do that, we're going to be giving a lot of secrets that we have that they [China] would want to have, or anybody else," he said.The announcement of the taskforce follows growing pressure from prominent figures in the industry, including executives of OpenAI and Anthropic, to tighten regulation of the technology.Trump first announced the taskforce in September, prompting Warren to state: "Congress cannot meet the pressing threat of AI by just forming another committee or continuing to have drawn-out discussions about it."She added: "Let's actually pass some meaningful regulations on AI to protect people."In an interview published on 4 October, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said the benefits of AI justify accepting some of its risks and argued that the technology should remain accessible to the public."The world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this ‌technology and people having the agency," Altman told Politico's technology-focused newsletter Decoded.The company recently admitted that a rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website in June and accessed private data.Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the agent "infiltrated" a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare.Despite the incident occuring in June, Albanese said the government only learned about the breach in August. He said there will be "legal consequences". OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon is due to appear as part of an AI inquiry in Australian on Tuesday.Over the weekend, a former leader in OpenAI's safety systems team wrote in an article for the Atlantic magazine that he had left the firm because its culture was "broken"."As [OpenAI] sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed," wrote David Robinson, who was involved in safety and transparency reporting.The BBC has contacted OpenAI for comment.Last month, the ChatGPT-maker pulled the release of its latest AI model due to safety concerns.Trump has largely left it to AI companies to regulate themselves.A pact signed on 29 September included the signatures of executives from top tech firms like OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and Google.On the same day, the president signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and should no longer acknowledge the use of the term artificial intelligence.SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.Some experts have questioned the logic of the rebranding, arguing that the use of "super intelligence" could cause confusion as it refers to more advanced systems.Some top tech leaders have already started to use the new name, including multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who said on social media on Sunday that he will rename his firm's AI platform SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI."SpaceX is a super intelligence company", Musk wrote.

schema.headline: Trump chooses top spy boss to run new AI taskforce

title: England confirm 50-over warm-up fixture at the Waca before Australia tour
description: With Jos Buttler and Adil Rashid injured, Joe Root was the only player in England's XI for the third ODI against Sri Lanka with more than 50 caps.Engl
body: With Jos Buttler and Adil Rashid injured, Joe Root was the only player in England's XI for the third ODI against Sri Lanka with more than 50 caps.England, who have struggled recently in 50-over cricket but have won three series in a row this year, have a minimum of 20 official ODIs before next year's World Cup in southern Africa."Aside from Jos, Joe and Adil Rashid, there's not a lot of experience in that side," McCullum said after victory over Sri Lanka. "We're going to try and put on a smattering of warm-up games to try and get guys up to speed as quickly as we can."England are also due to play warm-ups before their Test tours of South Africa and Bangladesh this winter, and before the one-off 150th anniversary Test against Australia in Melbourne in March.Those fixtures were in place before McCullum was replaced by Stephen Fleming as Test coach this summer. Since the Ashes, the ECB and Cricket Australia have held discussions about a reciprocal arrangement that would mean touring teams are provided with better preparation before Ashes series.England lost the first Ashes Test in Perth inside two days last year and were well beaten in the next two Tests to concede the series at the earliest opportunity. McCullum accepted afterwards mistakes may have been made with his side's preparation.England play three ODIs and five T20s in Australia this winter from 13 November to 2 December. They also play a 50-over tri-series in Pakistan against the hosts and Sri Lanka later this month.The announcement of England's new batch of central contracts, meanwhile, is expected to come next week, having initially been anticipated at the start of October.

schema.headline: England confirm 50-over warm-up fixture at the Waca before Australia tour

title: Brazil election goes to run-off as right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round
description: Right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro has won the first round of Brazil's presidential election, beating left-wing President Lula da Silva, but falling short of
body: Right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro has won the first round of Brazil's presidential election, beating left-wing President Lula da Silva, but falling short of an outright majority.There will be a run-off between the two candidates on 25 October.Bolsonaro is the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year prison sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election.Sunday's vote was close, with President Lula polling slightly ahead during the campaign. With almost all of the votes counted, Bolsonaro has 47% to Lula's 45% of the vote.Bolsonaro's result exceeded expectations, meaning the second round now looks like his to lose, given some of the other candidates knocked out in the first round were right-wing alternatives.Bolsonaro's Liberal Party (PL) also had the most governors, senators and federal deputies elected in the results so far, meaning the party is expected to have the most influence in Congress.The majority of Latin America has now elected right-wing presidents, aligned to the Trump administration, and the run-off will determine whether Brazil – Latin America's largest country and economy – will follow suit.After casting his ballot, Lula, 80, warned the choice was between democracy and "barbarism".Bolsonaro, 45, said he wanted to "free the Brazilian people".Lula and Bolsonaro are the two biggest names in Brazilian politics, on the left and right, and this campaign has polarised Brazil yet again: with themes of sovereignty, crime, the economy and corruption being top concerns for voters.Lula is more popular in Brazil's poorer northeast, among low-income voters, Catholics, and women.He is seeking a fourth term in office, after being elected in 2002, 2006 and then a later non-consecutive term in 2022. In that election, he beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% of the vote, the closest presidential election result in Brazil's history.After that election, Bolsonaro's supporters vandalised government buildings on 8 January 2023.Jair Bolsonaro was banned from running for re-election even before his prison sentence, but endorsed his eldest son Flávio to run in his place. Jair Bolsonaro's wife, Michelle, was elected to the Senate on Sunday.Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged to grant his father, and his supporters responsible for the 8 January riots, amnesty if elected.He is more popular in the south, and among wealthier voters and evangelical Christians.Bolsonaro said on Sunday he was "very happy" to have led Lula in the first-round vote, and expressed confidence that he would clinch a run-off victory in three weeks' time."I am very happy with the real possibility that, three weeks from now, Brazil will give a definitive answer by choosing a modern government," he said, according to AFP.Lula said the outcome of the vote was "unexpected", but insisted the race was not over."I admit I was convinced I would win in the first round," he said on Sunday. "The game is about to start. We are in extra time. In extra time, we will win over the Brazilian people."Corruption became a key issue in this campaign after a scandal involving a jailed banker, Daniel Vorcaro, who orchestrated one of Brazil's largest financial frauds, embroiling senior figures across the political spectrum.Bolsonaro acknowledged that he'd asked Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m).Lula was also impacted by the scandal indirectly, after police suggested Vorcaro had reached out to the Supreme Court judge Alexandre de Moraes to ask for help avoiding arrest. Moraes denies any wrongdoing.Moraes was not appointed by Lula but is seen as his ally, given Moraes presided over Jair Bolsonaro's coup trial.Crime and insecurity were also top concerns for voters. Brazil's homicide rate has fallen, but street crime such as phone thefts, that are highly visible to voters, have increased - and violence and drug trafficking are still major problems.Bolsonaro has pledged to designate Brazilian gangs as terrorists and build maximum-security prisons akin to those in El Salvador. His father, during his presidency, loosened gun ownership restrictions.Lula has criticised the US terrorist designation of Brazilian gangs but launched various reforms to tackle the financial networks of organised crime networks, improve homicide investigations, and invest in prisons.The economy has also been central to this campaign: the country has high levels of personal debt and slowing growth.Lula has defined his legacy through a series of social welfare programmes, most notably Bolsa Família, that pays families to ensure children stay in education and receive healthcare such as vaccines, as well as building more universities. The programmes have been credited with lifting millions of Brazilians out of poverty.He has also backed oil drilling exploration, which has proved controversial with environmentalists, but he has a record of tightening environmental protections and reducing the rate of deforestation in the Amazon. Deforestation increased significantly under Jair Bolsonaro's presidency.Flávio Bolsonaro has pledged a public debt ceiling and government spending cuts, a revision of social welfare, and to bolster the critical minerals sector.

schema.headline: Brazil election goes to run-off as right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round

title: NFL: Kansas City Chiefs, San Francisco 49ers & Minnesota Vikings stay unbeaten - week four round-up
description: Chiefs and 49ers remain unbeaten - five things from NFL week fourImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Kansas City Chiefs, San Francisco 49ers
body: Chiefs and 49ers remain unbeaten - five things from NFL week fourImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The Kansas City Chiefs, San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings are the only teams with a 4-0 recordByBen CollinsBBC Sport journalistOnly three teams remain unbeaten in the NFL after two more 100% starts were halted during week four of the season.Sunday's slate got under way with the Indianapolis Colts beating the Washington Commanders in the first of this season's three London games.The New England Patriots and Los Angeles Rams then avoided dropping to a 1-3 record by pulling off some big wins on the road.The Kansas City Chiefs and Las Vegas Raiders were among the five teams who made a 3-0 start to the season and one team's '0' had to go as the divisional rivals met, while the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings marched on.Here are five things you missed from Sunday's action.Raiders push Chiefs all the wayKansas City have dominated their rivalry with the Raiders in recent years, but Las Vegas are vastly improved after winning only three games last season and pushed the Chiefs all the way.The Raiders led 13-10 heading into the final quarter in Vegas, which featured three lead changes before Kansas City held on for a 30-27 win.The turning point came as new running back Kenneth Walker maintained his stunning start by scoring two touchdowns in 19 seconds, with the Chiefs regaining possession immediately by forcing a fumble on the kick-off return.The Raiders gave themselves hope with a Brock Bowers score and stayed alive until the final play, when Kirk Cousins was tackled as he threw and his wayward pass was intercepted.Walker finished with 177 yards from 22 carries, while team-mate Tyquan Thornton also had two touchdowns and 111 receiving yards.After missing last season's play-offs, the Chiefs look capable of getting back into Super Bowl contention. They next face the Los Angeles Chargers, who are 0-4 after losing 30-23 to defending champions the Seattle Seahawks.49ers and Vikings march onThe other two teams who improved to 4-0 were the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings.The 49ers hosted the Denver Broncos, who overcame Super Bowl favourites the Rams last week, and they were tied 3-3 until late in the third quarter.Christian McCaffrey's touchdown in the fourth quarter gave the 49ers some breathing space and, although Jaylen Waddle replied, George Kittle scored on a huge catch-and-run down the middle to seal a 24-14 win.While Cousins and Brock Purdy lead the league with 11 touchdown passes, Purdy has been intercepted only once and has not been sacked in the 49ers' first four games.The Vikings are the biggest surprise to be 4-0, having ground out another win, this time 15-10 over the Miami Dolphins, with Will Reichard kicking five field goals.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Drake Maye (right) was narrowly beaten by Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matt Stafford in voting for the 2025 Most Valuable Player awardMaye bounces backSome said Drake Maye's confidence was shot after he was benched during the New England Patriots' blowout loss at the Jacksonville Jaguars last week.After throwing eight interceptions in the 2025 regular season, the 24-year-old quarterback had six in the Patriots' first three games and only one touchdown pass.Next up was a daunting trip to the unbeaten Buffalo Bills - led by the 2024 Most Valuable Player Josh Allen - but Maye showed why he narrowly missed out on the MVP award last season, when he led the Patriots to an unexpected Super Bowl run.After Allen restored Buffalo's lead with a 34-yard touchdown pass to Keon Coleman with four minutes left, Efton Chism made a superb one-handed catch in the endzone to put the Patriots back in front.They then intercepted a hopeful Allen throw to clinch a 29-26 win, with Maye passing for three touchdowns and 269 yards.The Bills joined the Rams as Super Bowl favourites last week and they go head to head in LA next week.Another Eagles injury before London tripAfter losing a thriller at Denver last Monday, the LA Rams were 1-2 and faced another stern test on the road this week at the Philadelphia Eagles.The hosts led 20-10 at half-time after two Darius Cooper touchdowns, but the Rams fought back, with Kyren Williams rushing for two touchdowns in the final four minutes to claim a 24-20 victory.The fit-again Puka Nacua finished with 125 receiving yards and a touchdown for the Rams, while the Eagles' injury concerns mounted.Wide receiver DeVonta Smith (hamstring) was ruled out before the game, joining tight end Dallas Goedert (knee) on the sidelines, and Philadelphia lost star running back Saquon Barkley to an early hamstring injury.That is a big blow for the Eagles and UK fans as they visit Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday to face the Jacksonville Jaguars, who beat the Cincinnati Bengals 22-17 to make it back-to-back wins.The Baltimore Ravens also have fitness concerns over a key man, with two-time MVP Lamar Jackson (ankle) unable to play during the second half of their 24-18 home win against the Tennessee Titans.Cowboys continue to entertainThere have been at least 48 points in every Dallas Cowboys game this season, and they played their part in another high-scoring affair at state rivals Houston.The Texans led 23-13 after Nico Collins' second score in the third quarter and then 30-27 with two minutes remaining.But Dak Prescott led the Cowboys to a game-winning drive of 11 plays and 74 yards, throwing a touchdown pass to star receiver CeeDee Lamb to claim a 34-30 win.Lamb had a career-high 17 receptions for 189 yards, while team-mate Javonte Williams rushed for three touchdowns as Dallas improved to 2-2.Sunday's highest scorers were the New York Giants after Jameis Winston, filling in for injured quarterback Jaxson Dart, threw three touchdowns and two interceptions in a 36-24 win at home to the Arizona Cardinals.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, CeeDee Lamb leads the NFL for receiving yards with 498 from four games

title: Potty-training scheme to expand to more parts of England after city's success
description: Potty training scheme to roll out to 20 more areasImage caption, Parents like Natalie (right) say it's important children are confident enough to use
body: Potty training scheme to roll out to 20 more areasImage caption, Parents like Natalie (right) say it's important children are confident enough to use the loo on their own when they start schoolByKate McGoughEducation reporterUpdated 3 hours agoThe number of children who were toilet-trained before starting school this year has increased significantly in a city where parents were given potty training guides with their first school offers.York was the subject of the city-wide pilot, which also put on workshops for parents and offered special training for early years staff.Twenty local authorities across England are now signed up to launch similar schemes to tackle the number of pupils starting school without being fully toilet-trained.The government said the pilot's results were "encouraging", and confirmed they were committed to 75% of pupils reaching a good level of development at the end of their first year in school by 2028.Since April this year, parents across York have been targeted via GP surgeries, pharmacies, family hubs, schools, nurseries and libraries with information and offers of support on how to potty-train their child ahead of starting school. Potty training guides were sent out to all families across York who had a child starting reception in September - with the aim that all children could use the toilet independently by the time they started school, except those with medical issues or special educational needs. The results from all 55 mainstream primary schools across the city, shared exclusively with BBC News, suggested there had been a 43% drop since last year in the number of children who were not fully toilet-trained when they started school.Across York last September, 148 out of 1,364 reception pupils (11%) were recorded as not being toilet-trained when they started school. This year, that fell to 85 reception pupils out of 1,374 (6%).Parents Natalie and Lucy, who both have daughters starting reception next year, have welcomed the extra support on offer. Image caption, Mum Natalie says there's a lot of conflicting pressures on parents about the right time to potty-trainLucy said she had noticed the drop-in sessions on potty training in her local children's centre and thought it was a "really good idea". "I think it's really important that children are more prepared for that aspect of starting school," she said.Natalie said getting her daughter Freya potty-trained in time for school has been a priority, but feels there is a lot of pressure on parents to do so. "I think going to school is hard enough for children," she said."But for me it was really important that she's confident enough to use toilets, to be independent, to be able to go without relying on the help of teachers perhaps in an environment where they've already got lots of children to look after."Natalie said the popularity of disposable nappies might be a reason why parents often wait longer to potty train. "When I was little, we still had the terry towelling nappies and they had to be washed and hung on the line. So I think with disposable nappies it's easier," she said. Image caption, The ability to listen to and follow instructions is another skill that helps pupils get the most out of learning when they start reception classAround one in four children started school in England and Wales last year not fully toilet-trained, and teachers said they have been spending over an hour a day changing nappies, according to the latest research from the children's charity Kindred Squared, external.Felicity Gillespie, CEO of Kindred Squared, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that children not being potty trained when starting school was "a real concern for teachers". "They tell us that they're losing, on average across the country, a day a week of teaching time to dealing with potty-training issues."Gillespie is keen to spread the message that "it's best for children to be coming out of nappies" when they are between 18 and 30 months old. "When the teacher's leaving the class to change someone's nappy, the rest of the class is having their learning broken up. So everybody loses out,” she added.Jo Mould, who teaches reception at Robert Wilkinson Primary Academy in York, said she has noticed an improvement in pupils being ready for school this year. "We've spent more time teaching in these last three weeks than we have in previous years," she said."The children have come in so ready to learn, because they're more settled and regulated socially and emotionally. We've had a really, really positive start to the school year."Image caption, Jo Mould says not having to deal with toilet training has meant more time spent teaching her pupilsYork councillor Bob Webb said the impact of the scheme had been "so positive" for both schools and families.But he acknowledged a potential "gap in support" for parents between seeing health visitors with their toddler, and the child later arriving at school. He said the key to the scheme's success was collaboration across health visitors, schools and other community settings, but that there was "always more that could be done at an earlier age". Twenty local authorities across England have now committed to adopt York's model, developed by Kindred Squared, and use it to encourage earlier potty-training in their areas. They include: North LincolnshireSuffolkSolihullRotherhamHampshireHaltonLondon Borough of RedbridgeLondon Borough of HounslowCheshire West and ChesterJust over two-thirds of children in England (68.3%) leave reception class with a good level of development - a key measure of school readiness which includes things like communication skills, as well as physical, social and emotional development - according to the latest government stats, external. That means they were assessed by teachers on being able to complete tasks like going to the toilet and paying attention in class.The government has said it is still committed to increasing that proportion to 75% by 2028. Early Education Minister Paul Waugh said it was "encouraging to see this pilot helping more children develop the confidence and independence they need before starting school", stressing the importance of parents taking early steps towards toilet training.In York, Mould said she hopes next year's parents will take on potty-training even earlier. "Ideally we'd be at the point where [children] don't need that support when they get here, because they've already been trained by the time they get to us."Get in touchDo you have any views, comments or questions about this story?

schema.headline: Potty-training scheme to expand to more parts of England after city's success

title: Average five-year mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years
description: The average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6% for the first time in three years, figures show.The cost of home loans has
body: The average interest rate on a new five-year fixed mortgage deal has hit 6% for the first time in three years, figures show.The cost of home loans has been rising in recent weeks, as lenders face higher costs amid international concern over rising prices, interest rates, and government borrowing costs.It means home buyers and anyone renewing a fixed deal have seen about 1,500 mortgage deals priced below 5% vanish since the start of September, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.It described the situation as "brutal" for borrowers, with the average rate on five-year deals now at 6%, and at 5.98% on two-year fixed mortgages.For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals.Moneyfacts said that the biggest High Street lenders had made repeated fixed rate increases during September. Barclays increased selected fixed rates on four occasions, while HSBC, Lloyds Bank, Nationwide, NatWest, Santander and TSB each made three rounds of increases.It meant that the average rate on a new five-year deal was at its highest since September 2023. On two-year deals, the average rate is at its highest since December 2023."Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers," said Rachel Springall, finance expert at Moneyfacts."Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed."She said that those coming to the end of a fixed deal would be "wise to seek advice and compare deals carefully".Some lenders could allow people to lock in a rate three months before their current deal ends, while others could allow six months, she said.Springall said rate rises were "inevitable" because lenders' wholesale funding costs had climbed as a result of rising gilt yields.Interest rates - known as the yield - on government bonds have been going up, meaning it costs the government more to borrow over the long term.The knock-on impact of this on the mortgage market has meant that the number of fixed-rate deals priced below 5% has plunged by 99%, from 1,494 since the start of September 2026 to nine now.In contrast, the number of sub-5% variable rate mortgages has remained broadly stable, Springall said, leading some borrowers to chose deals that track the Bank of England's base rate.

schema.headline: Average five-year mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years

title: Cristiano Ronaldo: A nation divided as forward left with big decision on Portugal future
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, This sign praising Cristiano Ronaldo and criticising Jorge Jesus was placed outside Benfica's stadiumByEmlyn BegleyBBC
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, This sign praising Cristiano Ronaldo and criticising Jorge Jesus was placed outside Benfica's stadiumByEmlyn BegleyBBC Sport journalistAs Lionel Messi prepares to get a hero's farewell for his successful international career, Cristiano Ronaldo's could have ended with him running down the tunnel at the final whistle of a game he did not play.After the World Cup, Argentina's Messi, 39, decided to retire from international football, while Ronaldo, 41, opted to play on for Portugal.Yet there is the possibility that Messi's Argentina career will end up lasting a few days longer - with a home friendly with Benin on Tuesday marked as his final game.Ronaldo, furious at being made to warm up and not be brought on against Norway in the Nations League, walked out on the Portugal squad after finding out he would not start against Denmark either.The Al-Nassr forward has scored 146 goals and won 234 caps for Portugal - both world records.After such a high-profile falling-out with new boss Jorge Jesus, also a larger than life character who does not back down, Ronaldo is facing a big decision.Jesus has insisted he would be welcome back if he wants to return and talks between Ronaldo, his representatives and the Portuguese FA are ongoing as they look for a solution.While Ronaldo could not carry on playing forever, this is not how he would have expected his international career to end. His fans are remaining loyal to him, with social media full of posts supporting Ronaldo and criticising Jesus, while on the other side some fans and a lot of Portugal's media have been critical of what they see as selfish behaviour.Ahead of Portugal's next match against Denmark in November lies a big decision for one of the world's greatest ever players.What exactly happened?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jorge Jesus managed Cristiano Ronaldo at Saudi club Al-NassrIt has all happened very quickly.After the World Cup, Portugal replaced Roberto Martinez with Jesus, who had been Ronaldo's boss with Al-Nassr last season.Less than two weeks ago, Ronaldo said: "I had a conversation with our president, with our coach. I still believe that I'm able to help the national team to reach what they want."Things were still looking OK when he started in the 1-0 win over Wales.Jesus told Ronaldo he would be on the bench for the next game against Norway. After being told to warm up for a period of the game, he remained an unused substitute in a Portugal game for the first time in 18 years.Guillem Balague, who wrote a book about Ronaldo in 2015, said: "He gets asked to warm up for the whole of the second half, practically."There are tacit rules in football: you don't do that to Pele, to Diego Maradona, to Lionel Messi, to Cristiano, right? That's what he's seen, that you don't do that to those kind of players."And as the final whistle went he went down the tunnel instead of going to the fans with his team-mates.Jesus said there was no falling out - but confirmed Ronaldo would not start the next game with Denmark either.At that point Ronaldo left the training camp - and wrote on social media: "In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated."Portugal's FA president Pedro Proenca flew to Copenhagen, landing at 02:30 in the morning, to try to smooth things over with Ronaldo but failed.He has since said: "He is in the national team on sporting merit, and that must be unquestionable. We have to pay tribute to Ronaldo."After beating Norway on Sunday in their final Nations League match - again without Ronaldo - Jesus said: "If he wants to, he'll return to the national team. We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who's going to decide."He's the one who should decide how he wants to end his time with the national team."What do the fans think?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Some fans continue to support Cristiano RonaldoOn several billboards in Lisbon posters went up praising Ronaldo and criticising Jesus.They read, in Portuguese: "Thank you Cristiano Ronaldo for everything you did for Portugal. You will always be our captain. "Jorge Jesus was not up to the task. Lack of sensitivity. Treating a captain wrongly. Inflated ego."One was placed next to the Estadio da Luz, home of Benfica - who Jesus managed to three league titles.At the Denmark game, some fans wore T-shirts spelling out 'Love you Jesus' while others were head-to-toe in Ronaldo merch.Denmark striker Rasmus Hojlund, incidentally, celebrated his goal with his idol Ronaldo's trademark 'siuuu' - something he has done previously when netting against Portugal.Portugal's newspapers had differing perspectives.Record - who the forward owns shares in - said "Ronaldo leaves after clash with Jesus" and Jornal de Noticias said it was "the end of a historic era"."A sad goodbye," said Bola, while Jogo went for "CR7 turns his back on the national team".Meanwhile, videos were posted online of angry fans ripping up their Portugal jerseys.Jesus and Proenca were booed leaving a building in Copenhagen.But many foreign fans purely supported Portugal because of Ronaldo - so they do not necessarily represent the views of actual Portuguese supporters.Portugal fan Maria Ribeiro, from Lisbon, said: "It is so hard for all us fans. We all love him but it is getting too much now. It is hard to imagine Portugal without Ronaldo but maybe this is the time. There is too much arguing between ourselves."Would Portugal miss Ronaldo?Ronaldo's search for a record 1,000 career goals remains on but will he have to finish that at club level in Saudi Arabia?He has scored 979 times for Portugal, Sporting, Manchester United, Real Madrid, Juventus and Al-Nassr.While his old rival Messi scored eight goals, and assisted four more, to take Argentina to the summer World Cup final - Portugal fell at the last-16 stage.Ronaldo scored three goals in the tournament but failed to have an impact in their loss to Spain, leading BBC pundit Chris Sutton to say he was "waddling around the pitch like a grandad".Ronaldo's former United team-mate Wayne Rooney added: "He is a genius, a superstar. What he has given to football and millions of people is something very rare."He will be disappointed because he believed he could win this tournament. But time gets us all. It's a sad day for football."In the last nine years of Ronaldo's international career, Portugal's win percentage without him is slightly better - 64% to 63% - and they have scored 2.7 goals a game without him compared to 2.1 with him.The two biggest wins in their history - 9-0 over Luxembourg and 9-1 against Armenia - came in the last two qualifying matches that he missed, both through suspension.Journalist Marcus Alves, who covers Portugal, said: "How much gratitude is enough? That's a question that Portuguese fans have been asking for a few years now. "The whole soap opera that seems to follow the mere presence of the 41-year-old striker got to a point where patience was running out. "Of Portugal's last five coaches, Ronaldo had issues with four of them – Carlos Queiroz, Paulo Bento, Fernando Santos and now Jesus. That's too much distraction when Portugal have arguably their best generation ever."

schema.headline: Cristiano Ronaldo: A nation divided as forward left with big decision on Portugal future

title: Radical change needed to cut Scottish child poverty, says charity
description: Scotland is on course to miss legally-binding targets to cut child poverty "by a wide margin", according to a report from a leading social reform char
body: Scotland is on course to miss legally-binding targets to cut child poverty "by a wide margin", according to a report from a leading social reform charity.The Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF) said one in five children was in poverty and "radical change" was needed to put the Scottish government's pledges back on track.It urged ministers to craft a "much bolder and properly-funded plan to reduce poverty" by rewiring local government, public services and the tax system.The Scottish government said it had made great strides, with its policies keeping 100,000 children out of poverty this year, but accepted there was more to do.In 2017, MSPs passed a law requiring ministers to hit four targets, external, including pushing the share of children in relative poverty below 10% by 2030.But the JRF's Poverty in Scotland report, external found the figure remained stubbornly high, averaging 21% from 2022 to 2025. The UK average is 28%.Relative poverty means a household has disposable income after housing costs below 60% of the UK median, adjusted for family size and composition.Overall, the report concluded, 940,000 people in Scotland were in relative poverty – 17% of the population.In her statement, Somerville said tackling poverty was at the heart of the Scottish government's plans for public service reform including tailoring services for individual needs in an approach known as "whole-family support"."The time to go further is now," she said. "That means changing how services work together, ensuring they are joined up and designed around need, so that families can get the right support, at the right time and in the right place."The JRF describes the current roll-out and funding for whole-family support as "wholly inadequate."In a statement, Cosla, which represents local authorities, said its members took the report seriously and would do everything possible to cut poverty.But its resources spokesperson, Kelly Parry, said councils were being constrained by funding shortages and rising demand for services.Opinion polling conducted by the Diffley Partnership for the JRF suggests that two thirds of people think their council is underfunded, with just 4% saying the opposite.It also indicates that people significantly underestimate the 61% share of local government funding which comes directly from the Scottish government. Council tax, by contrast, accounts for just 17%.The pollster surveyed 3,381 adults in Scotland between 22 and 26 June."Councils are ready to be held accountable for the contribution we make," added Parry."But responsibility must be matched by the powers, fair and flexible multi-year funding, and genuine partnership needed to deliver lasting change."

schema.headline: Radical change needed to cut Scottish child poverty, says charity

title: Man City scandal shines light on Manchester United finances
description: United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we
body: United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn.To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m.Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027.  United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.The negativity around Manchester City's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a £10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.When Carrick sends his team out against bottom-club Tottenham at Old Trafford on 10 October, they will be attempting to drag themselves up from 12th place in the table.The overall target is undefined, but it is pretty clear Champions League qualification will be a significant part of it.

schema.headline: Man City scandal shines light on Manchester United finances

title: Dozens 'ripped off' across south of England in £500,000 building 'scam'
description: The couple said they paid a deposit of nearly £16,000 in March which they were told would cover architectural drawings and secure the last available s
body: The couple said they paid a deposit of nearly £16,000 in March which they were told would cover architectural drawings and secure the last available start date in June.But Simon said "alarm bells started blowing up in our heads" when the architect contacted them to say she had not been paid and would not release the drawings a week before work was due to start."We tried getting in contact with South Coast - they'd disconnected the phone, couldn't get through... my whole world just crumbled and it's a feeling that I never, ever want to experience again," said Simon.Sian added: "Having no control over that was really scary... the fact it can happen in an instant is really frightening."The couple have since joined an action group made up of 36 other customers who also claim to have paid SCC thousands of pounds for work that was not done.Simon said he had called his bank multiple times over two months before he finally got his money back in August.While 29 customers said they had managed to get their money refunded through their bank, eight have been told it is a civil matter and are having to go to the financial ombudsman service.On its website and social media pages, SCC claimed to be a leader in high-end construction, with customers telling the BBC they felt reassured by the number of accreditations it displayed online.But the BBC can reveal SCC was falsely claiming to be insured by Home Improvement Protection (HIP) and certified by Certass. In addition, it had only been a member of TrustATrader for six weeks in 2024.  A spokesperson for HIP said members must pay a premium to insure each customer contract. They said it had been brought to their attention that SCC had been advertising its membership certificate as proof of insurance, which was a "serious breach" of its terms of agreement. The company was expelled from the scheme in May.Several other accreditation memberships have been terminated, including Checkatrade in March and Which? Trusted Trader scheme in April.Accreditations from the Federation of Master Builders (FMB) and the government-backed TrustMark were ended in June following customer complaints.A spokesperson for FMB said: "This company joined the FMB in May 2025 after passing our rigorous vetting checks. When complaints started coming in and the company failed to respond to them, they were expelled in June 2026."The accreditation scheme providers all said checks had been carried out and SSC had passed the vetting process before receiving membership.A BBC investigation also found five outstanding county court judgments (CCJs) against SCC worth more than £37,000.CCJs indicate a company has not paid its debts and are red flags to customers and banks that a company could be in financial difficulty and might be at risk of collapse.The BBC understands 35 customers in the action group paid deposits for work that was not done between February 2025 and May 2026. The group said two customers had work started but not completed.According to Companies House, the sole director of SCC, Brandon Harris-Lee, 23, was appointed in July 2024.In a statement, he strongly denied scamming customers, highlighting what he described had been a successful trading history.He said: "We experienced significant problems on several projects including issues involving subcontractors, delays and substantial cost overruns."We were trying to generate income from ongoing and future work while simultaneously funding and completing projects that had significantly exceeded their budgets."Regarding the company's accreditations and insurance arrangements, certain bills and fees were not paid when they should have been as the company's financial position deteriorated."His cousin, Robert Lee, 28, had been a director at SCC between November 2024 and  October 2025.  He said in a statement that he "did not accept he deliberately took customers' money without intending for work to be carried out. We carried out a considerable amount of building work and, to my knowledge, had many satisfied customers during the period I was involved".A spokesperson for Sussex Police said: "We are investigating, alongside our partners, a number of reports of alleged fraud in connection with the company South Coast Construction (Sussex)."Anyone impacted or who has any information is asked to report to Sussex Police online, by calling 101 or using textphone 18001."

schema.headline: Dozens 'ripped off' across south of England in £500,000 building 'scam'
